kits.familyName: Checking sources before answering a question
setup: You work as {role|a} at {workplace|a}. {Lead|the} asked you to find out how {supply.plural} should be stored, and you found an answer online.
As {role|a} at {workplace|a}, you are researching the right way to store {supply.plural} for {lead|the}.
pressure: {coworker3} says the first search result is usually good enough.
{Lead|the} wants an answer by the end of the day.
detail: You searched on the break-room computer.
The answer will be posted in the stockroom.

fact: The answer you found comes from a company advertising its own storage cabinets.
issues.action: Compare the answer with the manufacturer's instructions or another independent source.
issues.reason: A company selling a product has a reason to slant its advice. An independent source tells you whether the claim holds up.
issues.lesson: Consider whether a source benefits from what it tells you.

shortcut.text: Use the answer, since the company knows a lot about storage.
shortcut.why: Expertise does not remove the interest in selling. The claim still needs checking.
shortcut.mis: A company's advertising is a neutral source.

fact: The guide you found was published eight years ago.
clear: You checked, and the guide was updated earlier this year.
issues.done: the guide was already confirmed as current
issues.action: Look for a current version before relying on it.
issues.reason: Products and guidance change. An eight-year-old guide may no longer be correct.
issues.lesson: Check that information is current before using it.

shortcut.text: Use it, since storage advice does not really change.
shortcut.why: Product formulas and packaging change. You need to confirm the advice is still current.
shortcut.mis: Older information is as good as new.

fact: The answer comes from an anonymous forum post that cites no source.
clear: The forum post links to the manufacturer's official storage instructions.
issues.done: the post already links to the official instructions
issues.action: Check the claim against an official or expert source before using it.
issues.reason: Anyone can post anything. An unsourced claim needs confirming before you rely on it.
issues.lesson: Verify claims that have no identifiable author or source.

shortcut.text: Use the post, since it has many likes.
shortcut.why: Popularity is not evidence. Many people can agree with a wrong claim.

fact: The source explains storage for home use, but your question is about storing large amounts at work.
issues.action: Find a source that covers storing large amounts at a workplace.
issues.reason: A reliable source can still be irrelevant. Storage at work may have different requirements.
issues.lesson: Make sure a source actually answers your question.

shortcut.text: Use the home advice, since storage is storage.
shortcut.why: Large amounts at work can raise issues home advice does not cover.
shortcut.mis: Any reliable source answers any related question.

fact: You plan to post the answer without saying where it came from.
issues.action: Include where the information came from when you share it.
issues.reason: Naming the source lets others check it and trust the answer.
issues.lesson: Share information with its source so others can check it.

shortcut.text: Leave out the source, since nobody will ask.
shortcut.why: Without the source, nobody can check the answer or update it later.

proceed.text: Share the answer with {lead|the}, along with where it came from.
proceed.why: The source is current, credible and relevant, so it is ready to share.
proceed.lesson: Share information once it is checked, and say where it came from.

generic.text: Ask {coworker2} what they think and post that instead.
generic.why: A coworker's opinion is not a checked source.
generic.mis: A coworker's guess is as good as research.

generic.text: Post several different answers so people can choose.
generic.why: Conflicting answers confuse people. Your job is to find the reliable one.
generic.mis: Giving every answer is the safest choice.

overcaution.text: Keep searching for another hour to be completely certain.
overcaution.why: The source already checks out. More searching delays the answer for little gain.
overcaution.mis: You can never check a source enough.

setup: {Lead|the} at {workplace|the} asked you to find reliable storage guidance for {supply.plural}.

steps.text: Write down exactly what you need to know
Check each source's author, date and purpose
Share the answer with its source

rel: A clear question makes searching faster and more relevant.
You evaluate sources after finding them.
Only share information that passed your checks.
process.lesson: Define the question, search, evaluate the sources, then share with credit.

title: Posted note: storing {supply.plural}
intro: You are checking this note before it is posted in the stockroom.
prompt: Which statement is not supported by reliable information?
doc.lesson: Information you share should be current, relevant, credible and credited.

lines.text: Store {supply.plural} in a cool, dry place off the floor.
Source: manufacturer's storage instructions, updated this year.

bad.text: Source: a forum post with no author listed.
bad.why: An anonymous post with no source is not reliable enough to post as guidance.

lines.text: Do not stack more than four boxes high, per the instructions.
lines.fine: A specific claim tied to the source.

bad.text: {supply.plural|cap} never expire, so dates do not matter.
bad.why: Nothing in the cited instructions supports this, and many supplies do expire.

lines.text: Keep the storage area labeled and organized.

bad.text: Tip from a home-organizing blog: store them under the kitchen sink.
bad.why: Home advice does not fit workplace storage, and the source is not relevant.

lines.fine: Tells readers where to go with questions.

bad.text: Questions: just do what seems right.
bad.why: Readers need someone to ask when the guidance is unclear.

review.notes: Source-evaluation criteria are not strictly ordered, so state issues are beginner-only; intermediate and advanced come from the data kit and document.

kits.familyName: Using data accurately in a report
setup: You work as {role|a} at {workplace|a}. {Lead|the} asked you to write a short report on last month's numbers for {task|the}.
As {role|a} at {workplace|a}, you are putting together a report on how {task|the} went last month.
pressure: {coworker3} says the report just needs to look good.
The report is due at the morning meeting.
detail: The data is in a shared spreadsheet.
The report will be one page long.

tiers.1: Using the wrong data makes every number in the report wrong.
tiers.2: Gaps in the data have to be understood before you calculate.
tiers.3: The report can only claim what the data shows.
tiers.4: Readers need to know where the numbers came from.

fact: The spreadsheet you were sent has last year's dates on every row.
clear: {coworker} confirmed the spreadsheet is last month's data.
issues.done: the spreadsheet was already confirmed as current
issues.short: the spreadsheet with last year's dates
issues.action: Ask {coworker} for the correct, current spreadsheet before you start.
issues.reason: A report built on the wrong year's data is wrong from the start.
issues.lesson: Make sure you have the right data before analyzing it.

shortcut.text: Use it anyway, since last year was probably similar.
shortcut.why: Last year's numbers do not describe last month, which is what the report is about.

fact: Several days in the spreadsheet are blank.
clear: {coworker} explained that the blank days were when {workplace|the} was closed.
issues.done: you already know why the days are blank
issues.action: Find out why those days are blank before calculating any totals.
issues.brief: find out why days are blank
issues.reason: Blanks could mean closures or missing records. The answer changes how you calculate the totals.
issues.lesson: Understand gaps in data before drawing conclusions from it.

shortcut.text: Count the blank days as zero and keep going.
shortcut.why: If the blanks are missing records, counting them as zero makes the totals wrong.

fact: {coworker2} wants the report to say results doubled, but the data shows a 20 percent rise.
issues.action: Report the 20 percent rise the data actually shows.
issues.reason: A report has to match its data. Overstating results misleads the people who decide based on it.
issues.lesson: Claim only what your data supports.

shortcut.text: Say results nearly doubled, since that sounds more impressive.
shortcut.why: A 20 percent rise is nowhere near double. The claim would mislead readers.

fact: Your draft does not say where any of the numbers came from.
issues.action: Add a line naming the spreadsheet and the dates it covers.
issues.reason: Naming the source lets readers check the numbers and trust the report.
issues.lesson: Say where your numbers come from.

shortcut.text: Leave it out, since everyone trusts your numbers.
shortcut.why: Trust is not a substitute for a source that others can check.

clear: Your draft already names the spreadsheet and the dates it covers.
issues.done: the source line is already in the draft

proceed.text: Write the report from the data and send it to {lead|the}.
proceed.why: The data is correct and understood, so the report can be written and shared.
proceed.lesson: Once the data checks out, report it accurately and clearly.

generic.text: Write the report from memory to save time.
generic.why: Memory is not data. The report needs the real numbers.
generic.mis: You remember the numbers well enough.

generic.text: Copy last month's report and change the date.
generic.why: Old numbers do not describe the new month.
generic.mis: Reports from month to month are interchangeable.

overcaution.text: Ask {lead|the} to recheck the whole spreadsheet before you begin.
overcaution.why: The data is already confirmed. A full recheck delays the report.
overcaution.mis: Data always needs a supervisor's check.

setup: You are preparing a short report on last month's numbers at {workplace|the}.

blanks: Some days in the data have no entries.
nosource: The report must say where its figures came from.

steps.text: Confirm you have last month's spreadsheet
Find out why some days are empty
Add a line naming the data source

rel: You check gaps in the right data.
How you treat the gaps changes the totals.
You calculate from the confirmed data.
You can only name the source once it is confirmed.
The source line goes into the finished report.
process.lesson: Confirm the data, understand its gaps, calculate, report, and cite.

review.notes: Use of information; numbers are qualitative (20 percent vs doubled).

setup: You work as {role|a} at {workplace|a}. {Lead|the} asked you to find out how often {equipment|the} should be serviced.
As {role|a} at {workplace|a}, you are researching the right service schedule for {equipment|the}.
pressure: {coworker3} says to just pick whichever answer sounds right.
detail: The current schedule was set years ago.
You have about an hour for this.

tiers.1: The most authoritative source should settle a disagreement.
tiers.2: A source has to match your exact equipment.
tiers.4: A coworker's memory should be checked against the source.
tiers.5: Share the answer with where it came from.

fact: Two websites give different service schedules for {equipment|the}.
issues.action: Check the manufacturer's manual for {equipment|the}, the most authoritative source.
issues.reason: The manufacturer knows the equipment best. Its manual settles what random websites disagree about.
issues.lesson: When sources conflict, go to the most authoritative one.

shortcut.text: Pick the website that appears first in the search.
shortcut.why: Search ranking is not a measure of accuracy.
shortcut.mis: The first result is the most reliable.

fact: The manual you found is for a different model of {equipment}.
issues.short: the manual for a different model
issues.action: Find the manual for your exact model before using its schedule.
issues.reason: Different models can need different service schedules.
issues.lesson: Make sure a source fits your exact situation.

shortcut.text: Use it, since the models are probably similar.
shortcut.why: Similar is not the same; schedules can differ by model.

clear: You confirmed the manual matches the model number on {equipment|the}.
issues.done: the manual already matches your model

fact: The manual page you are using is from an older printing.
issues.action: Check whether an updated version of the manual exists.
issues.reason: Manufacturers update schedules; an older printing may be out of date.

shortcut.text: Use it, since manuals rarely change.
shortcut.why: Schedules do get revised. A quick check prevents relying on old guidance.

clear: The manufacturer's site shows this is the latest version of the manual.
issues.done: the manual is already confirmed as the latest

fact: {coworker} insists the schedule learned years ago is still right.
issues.action: Thank {coworker}, and compare that schedule with the current manual.
issues.reason: Experience is valuable but memory can be outdated; the manual confirms it.
issues.lesson: Check remembered information against a reliable source.

shortcut.text: Go with {coworker}'s schedule, since experience beats manuals.
shortcut.why: Memory can be outdated or mistaken; it needs checking.

fact: You plan to tell the team the schedule without saying where it came from.
issues.action: Share the schedule along with the manual page it came from.
issues.reason: Naming the source lets others check it and update it later.

shortcut.text: Just tell everyone the schedule, since the source does not matter.
shortcut.why: Without the source, nobody can verify or update the schedule.

proceed.text: Share the manual's schedule, and where it came from, with {lead|the}.
proceed.why: The source is authoritative, relevant and current, so the answer is ready.
proceed.lesson: Share information once you know it is reliable, relevant and current.

generic.text: Average the different schedules you found.
generic.why: Averaging conflicting sources produces a number nobody recommended.
generic.mis: Averaging conflicting information makes it accurate.

generic.text: Ask {lead|the} to decide without telling them what you found.
generic.why: The lead asked you to research it; withholding the findings wastes the work.
generic.mis: Research should end with someone else deciding blind.

overcaution.text: Call the manufacturer to confirm the manual says what it says.
overcaution.why: The manual is already current and matches your model; calling adds nothing.
overcaution.mis: No written source can be trusted.

title: Service schedule note for {equipment|the}
intro: Check this note before it is posted next to {equipment|the}.
prompt: Which statement is not supported by reliable information?
doc.lesson: Posted guidance should come from the authoritative, current source for your exact equipment.

lines.text: Service every 90 days, per the manufacturer's manual.
Manual matches the model number on the label.

bad.text: Manual is for a similar model; ours should be about the same.
bad.why: A different model's manual may not apply.

lines.text: Manual version: latest, checked this month.

bad.text: Manual version: an old printing we found in a drawer.
bad.why: An old printing may have outdated guidance.

lines.text: Questions: see the manual or ask {lead|the}.

bad.text: Questions: search online and use any answer that sounds right.
bad.why: Unvetted online answers are not reliable guidance.

lines.text: Next service due: 90 days after the last entry in the log.

bad.text: Next service due: once a year.
bad.why: This contradicts the manual's 90-day schedule stated above.

review.notes: Source evaluation with an explicit priority: authority, relevance, currency, corroboration, citation.
